paras: The pursuit of a Black man in Chester County, Pennsylvania, was a manhunt by a crowd of white residents in about June 1903 after the man was said to have shot and killed a farmer. No report of its outcome appears in the coverage, and the episode is known only from a Maryland editorial that cited it as evidence that lynching had spread to the North.

According to the Democratic Advocate of Westminster, Maryland, the pursuit took place "at the same time" as the lynching of a Black man near Wilmington, Delaware, "a few weeks" before the paper's issue of 11 July 1903. The same editorial grouped it with other northern cases of that summer, among them a lynching and riot at Evansville, Indiana, and an attempted lynching at Asbury Park, New Jersey, that police prevented.

The editorial's only statement on the episode is that "a crowd of whites in Chester county, Pa., were after a negro who had shot and killed a farmer." It does not name the accused man, the farmer or the town, and it gives no date for the killing or the pursuit. Nor does it say whether the man was caught, harmed, arrested or tried.

The episode appears in the coverage only in the Democratic Advocate's editorial "The North Takes Up Lynching," printed on page 2 on 11 July 1903. The editorial opened by arguing that "curtailment of negro suffrage" in the South had reduced assaults on white women, so that northern papers had "little use" for the headline "A Southern Outrage." It then turned to northern cases, declaring that "Lately the North has gotten into the lynching business," and stated the alleged killing of the farmer as fact.
No news report of the farmer's killing or the manhunt, and no Black-press account of it, was found.

accounts.label: Maryland editorial
accounts.gist: A few weeks before 11 July 1903, at the same time as a lynching near Wilmington, a crowd of whites in Chester County, Pa., was after a Black man who had shot and killed a farmer.

framing.detail: Under the headline 'The North Takes Up Lynching', the Democratic Advocate used northern cases, this one among them, to answer northern criticism of the South, opening with a defense of Black disfranchisement and treating the alleged killing as fact.
